title: Psalm 51: Create in Me a Clean Heart
summary: David pleads for mercy after his sin with Bathsheba, appealing to God's loving devotion and great compassion. He confesses his guilt without excuse, asks to be washed, purified, and made new, and prays not to lose God's presence or Holy Spirit. He promises to teach sinners God's ways and offers God what he truly desires, a broken and contrite heart, before closing with a prayer for Jerusalem.
story: Psalm 51 is the most famous prayer of repentance in the Bible, and it opens the second collection of David's psalms (51 to 72), which ends with the note "Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse" (Psalm 72:20). It follows Psalm 50's warning that God wants thanksgiving and obedience more than sacrifice, and it answers with a king who has broken God's law and knows no sacrifice can fix it. The story behind it, told in 2 Samuel 11 and 12, is a turning point in David's life: from that point his family and kingdom are troubled, yet God does not withdraw his covenant promise. The psalm shows what the way back to God looks like.
historical:
The heading ties the psalm to the time when Nathan the prophet confronted David after his adultery with Bathsheba. According to 2 Samuel 11 and 12, David slept with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, one of his soldiers, while Uriah was at war. When she became pregnant, David tried to cover it up and then arranged Uriah's death in battle. Nathan exposed him with a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb, and David confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). This would place the psalm in David's reign, around the early tenth century BC.

Many scholars regard the psalm's headings as early editorial notes rather than original to the poems, and some date the psalm later, especially verses 18 and 19, which pray for the walls of Jerusalem to be rebuilt. Those verses may have been added during or after the exile, when the walls lay in ruins and sacrifice had ceased, adapting David's prayer for a nation in need of forgiveness. Others read them as David's own prayer that his sin would not bring ruin on the city. Either way, the church and synagogue have always read the psalm alongside David's story.
cultural:
Hyssop (verse 7) was a small aromatic plant whose branches were used for sprinkling in rituals of purification: to smear the Passover blood (Exodus 12:22), to cleanse a person healed of a skin disease (Leviticus 14), and to sprinkle the water that removed defilement from contact with the dead (Numbers 19). David asks God himself to perform the cleansing a priest would normally carry out. Bloodguilt (verse 14) was the guilt of having shed innocent blood, which in Israel's law could not be atoned for by ordinary sacrifice. Uriah's murder lies behind the word.

The law provided sacrifices for unintentional sins, but deliberate sins like adultery and murder carried the death penalty, with no sacrifice prescribed (Numbers 15:30-31). This is why David says God does not delight in sacrifice (verse 16): there was nothing he could bring. His only hope was God's mercy.
literary: The psalm opens with a cluster of words for sin (transgression, iniquity, sin) and words for cleansing (blot out, wash, cleanse), piled up to cover sin from every angle. Verses 1 to 9 are confession and plea for cleansing; verses 10 to 12 ask for inner renewal, with the word spirit appearing three times; verses 13 to 17 promise witness and praise; verses 18 and 19 widen the prayer to Zion. The phrase "blot out" in verses 1 and 9 frames the first section. The verb "create" in verse 10 is the same one used in Genesis 1, which in this stem takes only God as its subject.

outline.t: A plea for mercy and cleansing
Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow
A clean heart and a right spirit
Praise and the sacrifice of a broken heart

doctrines.note: The psalm gives repentance its classic shape: full admission of guilt without excuse, appeal to God's mercy rather than one's own merit, desire for inner change, and a life of witness to follow.

Sin is named in three words (transgression, iniquity, sin) and traced back to birth (verse 5). It is first of all an offense against God, and it reaches the inward parts, requiring a new heart, not merely a changed record.

"Take not Your Holy Spirit from me" is one of only a few places in the Old Testament that speak of God's Holy Spirit (the others are in Isaiah 63:10-11). David, who had seen the Spirit depart from Saul (1 Samuel 16:14), prays not to share Saul's fate.
No sacrifice was prescribed for David's sins, so the psalm throws itself on God's mercy. It shows that forgiveness finally rests on God's own provision, not on what the sinner can offer.

words.note: Bara, to create. In the simple stem used here, only God is ever the subject of this verb. David does not ask God to repair his heart but to create a new one, as he created the world. Repentance is not self-improvement but a new work of God.
Machah, to wipe or blot out, used of erasing writing from a scroll and of the flood wiping out life (Genesis 7:23). David asks God to wipe out the record of his transgressions (verses 1 and 9).

Ruach, spirit, breath, or wind. It appears in verses 10, 11, 12, and 17: a right spirit, God's Holy Spirit, a willing spirit, a broken spirit. The psalm moves between the human spirit and God's Spirit, which alone can renew it.
Dakhah, to crush. It describes the bones God has crushed (verse 8) and the contrite heart (verse 17). The same crushing that David feels as judgment becomes the humility God welcomes.

christ: Paul quotes verse 4 in Romans 3:4 to show that God is right when he judges, even if every human being is found false. The psalm's longing for a clean heart and a renewed spirit finds its answer in the new covenant promise of Ezekiel 36:26-27 and Jeremiah 31:33, which the New Testament says Christ inaugurates. David's plea for cleansing that no sacrifice could provide points toward the one sacrifice that cleanses completely: Hebrews says the blood of Christ purifies the conscience in a way animal blood could not (Hebrews 9:13-14), and 1 John 1:9 promises that God will cleanse from all unrighteousness those who confess their sins.

hard.q: How can David say "Against You, You only, have I sinned" when he wronged Bathsheba and murdered Uriah?
hard.a: David is not denying that he harmed people. In 2 Samuel 12 he accepts Nathan's rebuke about Uriah without dispute. Most interpreters read verse 4 as saying that sin is at root an offense against God, whose law protects neighbors; every wrong done to a person is also a wrong done to the one whose image they bear. Some take it as hyperbole meant to express how David now sees his guilt: before God, all excuses fall away. Others note the courtroom language of the verse: God is the only judge who can pronounce a verdict, so David addresses his confession to him. None of these readings make the harm to others less; they place it under the gaze of God.

questions: David offers no excuses in this psalm. What excuses do you tend to reach for when you are confronted with your own wrongdoing?
What is the difference between asking God to clean up your record and asking him to create a clean heart in you?
"A broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise." How does that promise speak to someone who thinks they have gone too far?
